courses.title: 1. Your first Qt desktop application
courses.summary: Choose a desktop kit, configure a CMake project, and understand how a C++ application becomes a responsive window.

lessons.title: Qt, C++ and the desktop kit
paragraphs: Qt is a set of C++ libraries and tools. Qt Creator is an IDE that can edit and build Qt projects; it is not the library itself. A desktop kit selects a compiler, Qt build, debugger and target architecture. Windows, macOS and Linux need compatible native kits, even when they share the same source.

Use Qt 6.5 or newer with C++17 and CMake for these projects. Install Widgets and Test first, then the modules named in each README. On Windows, keep an MSVC Qt kit with MSVC and a MinGW kit with MinGW. On macOS select a kit for your architecture; on Linux install the platform and development dependencies required by your distribution.
lessons.example:
source C++ + Qt headers -> compiler -> object files
object files + matching Qt libraries -> linker -> executable
executable + platform plugins -> desktop window
lessons.pitfall: Installing only Qt Creator leaves you without the matching Qt libraries and compiler needed to build the downloaded app.

question.prompt: What does a Qt desktop kit bring together?

options.text: A compatible compiler, Qt build and target architecture

question.explanation: The kit is the native toolchain configuration, not just the editor.

lessons.title: Configure, build and run
paragraphs: CMake configuration finds dependencies and creates a build system; compilation happens in the next step. Keep generated files in a separate build directory. Each course ZIP supplies CMakeLists.txt, the lesson sources and tests, so you can open that file directly in Qt Creator rather than copying snippets into an unrelated template.

The imported Qt6::Widgets target supplies include directories and link settings. qt_standard_project_setup enables the automatic Qt code-generation steps. Record the Qt version and build configuration when a result matters: running an old executable after a failed build can make a broken change appear successful.
lessons.example:
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="<your Qt kit>"
cmake --build build --config Debug
ctest --test-dir build -C Debug --output-on-failure
lessons.pitfall: A successful CMake configure does not prove compilation or application behavior; inspect the build exit status and run the tests.

question.prompt: Which command performs compilation after configuration?
question.explanation: Build invokes the generated native build system.

lessons.title: The application and event loop
paragraphs: Construct one QApplication before creating Widgets. The top-level window is a local C++ object that remains alive while app.exec runs. show requests a visible window; exec dispatches events such as painting, keyboard input and button clicks until the application exits. Returning from main immediately would destroy the window.

The first project connects a button to a counter label. No polling loop is needed: Qt calls the connected handler when the user clicks. Keep handlers short so the same event loop can redraw and respond to input. Closing the last ordinary window normally ends the application.
lessons.pitfall: Putting an endless while loop before exec prevents Qt from processing the events required to display and operate the window.

question.prompt: Why must the application enter exec()?

options.text: To dispatch GUI and other application events

question.explanation: The event loop delivers input, paints and queued callbacks.

lessons.title: Read the first useful diagnostic
paragraphs: Distinguish configure errors, compiler errors, linker errors and runtime deployment errors. Missing Qt6Config.cmake is a discovery problem. An unknown identifier is a compiler problem. An unresolved definition is a linker problem. A missing platform plugin can occur only after a binary was built and launched.

Build the unedited example first, click three times and then change the label wording. If behavior does not change, check the launched binary path and rebuild. The supplied test verifies the actual counter response. Testing on one host establishes that host result; use the deployment course to validate other target systems.
lessons.example:
Expected manual check:
launch -> Clicks: 0
click three times -> Clicks: 3
close window -> process exits
lessons.pitfall: Copying random library files into the project can hide a kit mismatch; fix the toolchain or deployment configuration at its source.

question.prompt: An app builds but reports a missing platform plugin at launch. Which stage failed?
question.explanation: The executable exists, but its runtime dependencies are incomplete.

Extract the ZIP into a new folder. Open CMakeLists.txt in Qt Creator or configure with the README command.
Build, launch, and click the counter three times. Resize and close the window.
Run CTest, change the greeting, rebuild and confirm the new executable is the one being launched.

A passing reset test and a deliberate failing assertion.

questions.explanation: Behavior must be exercised, not inferred from configuration.

courses.title: 2. C++ ownership and the Qt object model
courses.summary: Manage object lifetimes, value types, custom signals and lambda captures without dangling UI references.

lessons.title: Value types and application data
paragraphs: Keep task information as data: a QString title, a bool for completion and a stable identifier. Passing a value into a function makes its lifetime easier to reason about than retaining a reference to a temporary input field. QString uses UTF-16 code units; an 80-unit limit is not a promise of 80 visible characters.

Qt containers and strings provide value semantics. Implicit sharing may defer copying until modification, but it does not make concurrent mutation of one instance safe. The examples use local snapshots when work outlives the click handler and validate title length before accepting data.
lessons.pitfall: A reference to input->text() cannot be treated as a durable pointer to future input; capture a value snapshot when a callback needs owned data.

question.prompt: What does QString::size measure here?

options.text: Always the number of visible characters

question.explanation: Unicode display characters can span more than one UTF-16 unit.

lessons.title: Parent ownership and ordinary RAII
paragraphs: Heap-allocated child QObjects are deleted when their parent is destroyed. A window can own a controller and controls so their lifetimes match the UI. Qt also supports ordinary stack lifetime, but construction order matters if stack objects are parented: never let a parent try to delete a stack child that still has an independent lifetime.

Choose one clear ownership strategy. Use parent ownership for the lesson controller and Qt controls; use normal C++ values for data and RAII for non-QObject resources. A raw pointer to a parent-owned child is an observing handle. It does not mean the code should delete it again during routine shutdown.
lessons.pitfall: Wrapping a parent-owned QObject in another owning mechanism can produce competing owners and double deletion.

question.prompt: Who normally deletes a heap child QObject?

options.text: The garbage collector in the browser
Its parent when the parent is destroyed

question.explanation: QObject maintains an ownership tree for parented children.

lessons.title: Q_OBJECT and custom signals
paragraphs: CounterController derives from QObject, declares Q_OBJECT, and exposes increment and countChanged. moc generates meta-object support during the build. A signal reports a state transition to interested objects without making the controller depend on a particular label or window design.

Keep the controller in a listed header so AUTOMOC sees it. Changing count updates the stored value and emits one notification. Consumers can observe state without copying the increment algorithm. The test uses QSignalSpy to verify both emitted values and the number of transitions.
lessons.pitfall: Omitting Q_OBJECT or moc processing for a class with custom signals leads to missing meta-object behavior or unresolved symbols.

question.prompt: What generates meta-object support for a Q_OBJECT class?
question.explanation: CMake AUTOMOC arranges the required code generation.

lessons.title: Context objects and lambda lifetime
paragraphs: The context-taking connect overload ties a callback to a receiver object. When that context is destroyed, Qt disconnects the callback. This is a lifetime rule for the connection, not an ownership guarantee for every pointer captured by the lambda. Captured objects must also remain valid.

The example captures the label pointer whose parent is the same live window used as context. Avoid broad reference captures for delayed work because local variables disappear when the enclosing function returns. For a QObject whose lifetime differs, use QPointer and check it before use; for plain data, capture owned values.
lessons.pitfall: A context-free callback capturing a short-lived local reference can execute after that local has been destroyed.

question.prompt: Why supply the window as a connection context?

options.text: The callback disconnects when that window is destroyed
It makes every captured raw pointer immortal
It runs every callback on a new thread

question.explanation: Context lifetime controls connection lifetime and delivery context.

options.text: No, each captured object still needs a valid lifetime

questions.explanation: Connection lifetime and captured object lifetime are distinct.

courses.title: 3. Widgets, layouts and Qt Designer
courses.summary: Build an adaptive form with labels, size policies, tab order and a real Designer .ui file.

lessons.title: Let layouts calculate geometry
paragraphs: A desktop form must accommodate different window sizes, fonts and translated labels. Layout managers calculate geometry from each control's size hints and policies. A form layout pairs labels and fields; box layouts stack groups. Fixed positions may look correct at one size but overlap after a font or language change.

The downloaded Form.ui contains a vertical layout with a labeled input, a Save button and a status label. The layout owns the arrangement while the window owns the widgets. Resize the form and observe which control expands. A sensible minimum size should protect readability without forbidding useful resizing.
lessons.example:
QVBoxLayout -> title label, input, Save, status
QFormLayout -> paired labels and fields
QSizePolicy::Expanding -> may consume extra room
lessons.pitfall: Setting geometry manually on controls managed by a layout creates competing layout decisions.

question.prompt: Who should calculate child positions in an adaptive form?
question.explanation: Layouts respond to available space and control size hints.

lessons.title: The .ui file is source
paragraphs: Qt Designer stores the form as XML. During the build, uic generates ui_Form.h, which provides setupUi. The C++ application includes that generated header and calls setupUi on a live widget. Keep Form.ui in source control; generated headers belong in the build directory.

Open the exact Form.ui in Designer, change the status label, then rebuild. The generated code can change completely when the form changes, so business rules do not belong in ui_Form.h. Put event handling and validation in the maintained C++ class or controller instead.
lessons.pitfall: Editing ui_Form.h loses changes on the next build because uic regenerates that file.

question.prompt: Which file should you edit to change the authored Designer layout?
question.explanation: The .ui document is the maintained source of the layout.

lessons.title: Labels, focus and input
paragraphs: Give fields meaningful accessible names and use label buddies so keyboard users can reach the input through a mnemonic. Establish a tab order that follows the visible task. Placeholder text is a hint, not a replacement for a persistent label; it disappears as soon as a user starts typing.

In the sample the Task title label points to titleInput. The Save button also has a keyboard mnemonic. Test typing, Tab and activation without a mouse. Platform conventions differ, so record behavior on each target OS instead of assuming one keyboard screenshot proves accessibility everywhere.
lessons.example:
label text: &Task title
buddy: titleInput
tab order: titleInput -> saveButton
status label: wraps text inside the form
lessons.pitfall: Removing labels because placeholder text looks cleaner makes the form harder to identify after data entry and for assistive technology.

question.prompt: What does a label buddy provide?

options.text: A relationship that can move focus to its input

question.explanation: A buddy links a label and input for keyboard access.

lessons.title: Responsive feedback without losing drafts
paragraphs: Validation messages should explain how to proceed while preserving the typed value. The sample accepts a nonempty trimmed title and displays it as plain text. Qt labels can auto-detect rich text, so user-provided titles should use Qt::PlainText when interpreted markup is not part of the feature.

Try a title containing angle brackets, then resize the window until the status wraps. The content should remain literal and readable. Visual inspection should include long input, a large system font and keyboard traversal. The automated test checks form object names and actual Save behavior, while manual checks cover layout at real display settings.
lessons.pitfall: Displaying a user title in an auto-rich-text label can interpret markup instead of showing the literal title.

question.prompt: How should a status label display an ordinary user title?

options.text: As plain text with readable wrapping

question.explanation: Plain text preserves literal input and avoids accidental markup.

courses.title: 4. Signals, slots and validated forms
courses.summary: Connect user intent to reusable C++ rules, preserve invalid drafts, and distinguish signals from low-level events.

lessons.title: Typed connections and user intent
paragraphs: A signal describes something that happened, such as clicked or textChanged. A slot or compatible lambda handles it. Use the typed connect overload so the compiler checks compatible signatures. Wire each intended action once during construction rather than reconnecting every time a button is pressed.

The form connects Add task and Return in the title input to the same button action. One action calls the same validator and creates one row. This keeps mouse and keyboard paths consistent. Multiple accidental connections can execute one handler more than once, so behavioral tests must count rows after a single action.
lessons.example:
connect(input, &QLineEdit::returnPressed, addButton, &QPushButton::click);
connect(addButton, &QPushButton::clicked, this, [this] { addDraft(); });
lessons.pitfall: Reconnecting on every click accumulates callbacks and can create several tasks from one later click.

question.prompt: How should keyboard Return and Add button activation reach validation?
question.explanation: Shared actions keep input methods consistent.

lessons.title: Validate at the mutation boundary
paragraphs: The accepted task-title rule rejects empty or whitespace-only input, control characters, and more than 80 UTF-16 units. Accepted titles are trimmed before storage. The task collection is bounded to 100 items for this teaching app. Field hints help learners but the model must enforce the rules when data is actually changed.

An input widget limit cannot protect file imports or other callers. The shared Task.h rule is used by the model and persistence path. Validate the original value before trimming so an embedded control character cannot disappear and become an accepted value through a different route.
lessons.pitfall: Checking only that text is nonempty accepts strings consisting of spaces and misses invalid imported values.

question.prompt: Where must task rules be enforced?

options.text: At every accepted state mutation boundary

question.explanation: All input paths must obey the same accepted data contract.

lessons.title: Draft, accepted state and feedback
paragraphs: The text field contains a draft, which can be incomplete or invalid. The model holds accepted tasks. A failed Add should keep the draft visible and leave the model unchanged. A successful Add clears the draft and moves focus back to it so another task can be entered without extra mouse movement.

The status label explains the outcome rather than silently disabling all recovery. It renders ordinary text. The native tests try blank input, whitespace and a valid title, then inspect actual row counts. State transitions matter more than whether a button happens to be painted green.
lessons.example:
blank draft -> Add -> same draft, zero new rows
valid draft -> Add -> one accepted row, cleared input
invalid edit -> accepted task stays unchanged
lessons.pitfall: Clearing an invalid draft forces the user to recreate it and conceals the value that caused the validation failure.

question.prompt: What should happen after an invalid Add?

options.text: Create an empty row for later repair
Keep the draft and accepted collection unchanged

question.explanation: Invalid input must not mutate accepted data.

lessons.title: Signals versus events
paragraphs: Qt events include low-level input and lifecycle notifications; signals are higher-level object notifications. Prefer clicked, returnPressed and textChanged for ordinary form behavior. Override an event handler only when a specific event contract is needed, and preserve base behavior when your handler does not consume the event.

Event filters can observe another object's events, but returning true consumes the event and can accidentally break typing or focus. For this form no global key interception is needed. The next course uses closeEvent because closing a dirty document is a lifecycle decision requiring an explicit accept or ignore response.
lessons.example:
ordinary form: clicked -> validated action
window lifecycle: closeEvent -> accept or ignore
eventFilter returns true -> event is consumed
lessons.pitfall: A global key filter that consumes every key can prevent controls from editing text or performing their normal keyboard actions.

question.prompt: When is a closeEvent override useful?

options.text: When window closing must respect unsaved work

question.explanation: Close is a lifecycle event with an accept-or-ignore decision.

courses.title: 5. Main windows, actions and dialogs
courses.summary: Build a document editor shell with menus, reusable actions and explicit decisions about unsaved work.

lessons.title: A main window has dedicated regions
paragraphs: QMainWindow already manages a central widget, menu bar, status bar, toolbars and dock areas. Put your document editor in setCentralWidget rather than installing another top-level layout on QMainWindow. The native example uses a QPlainTextEdit so its text stays literal and editable.

An action represents an operation, such as New or About. Its text, shortcut and enabled state can be shared by a menu and toolbar. This makes the operation consistent regardless of where it is invoked. The sample uses standard key sequences where possible to respect desktop conventions.
lessons.pitfall: Installing a layout directly on QMainWindow competes with its existing management of central and dock regions.

question.prompt: Where should a main document widget go?

options.text: In a replacement layout on QMainWindow itself

question.explanation: QMainWindow owns dedicated layout regions.

lessons.title: Model the dirty state
paragraphs: A document is dirty when accepted edits differ from the last saved or explicitly new state. QPlainTextEdit exposes document modification state. Reflect it in the window title and consult it before an action would discard work. The sample is intentionally an in-memory editor; this course does not yet save to disk.

New can clear a clean document immediately, but a dirty document must ask whether to discard or cancel. Cancel must leave both text and dirty state unchanged. Opening a confirmation is not equivalent to a successful save; only the later file course can clear dirty state after an actual successful write.
lessons.pitfall: Clearing dirty state before knowing whether a save succeeded can falsely tell the user that their work is protected.

question.prompt: What must Cancel preserve when New would discard edits?

options.text: The current text and its dirty state

question.explanation: Cancel means the pending replacement did not happen.

lessons.title: Make dialog outcomes explicit
paragraphs: A dialog has a purpose and a result. A confirmation names the action and offers clear choices. The editor sample uses a synchronous question for this short teaching flow. More complex applications should consider open with a result signal so they avoid creating a nested event loop with exec.

An asynchronously opened dialog must outlive the function that opens it. A stack-local dialog followed by open is destroyed as the function returns. Use an appropriate parent and owned lifetime, and handle accepted/rejected signals with a context. Never treat a rejected dialog as acceptance merely because time passed.
lessons.pitfall: A local QDialog destroyed immediately after open never provides a usable asynchronous interaction.

question.prompt: What is required for a dialog opened asynchronously?

options.text: A blocking sleep in the caller
A temporary pointer to a destroyed local dialog
A lifetime that extends until the dialog completes

question.explanation: The UI object must remain alive while the user interacts.

lessons.title: Close is a cancellable transition
paragraphs: Closing the window is another operation that can discard work. closeEvent asks the same decision helper used by New and then accepts or ignores the event. This centralizes the policy while leaving the different operations responsible for their own state changes.

The native test types text, triggers New, selects Cancel and verifies the document is intact. It then chooses Discard and verifies an empty clean document. Test the OS close button separately too; a menu test alone does not establish that the close event reaches the same policy.
lessons.pitfall: Handling only File > New leaves the window close button as an unprotected data-loss path.

question.prompt: Which decision should a cancelled close apply?

options.text: Accept the event and restore text later

question.explanation: Ignoring prevents the window from closing.

courses.title: 6. Model/view, editing and filtering
courses.summary: Create a real QAbstractListModel with stable task identity, edit notifications and correct proxy-to-source selection.

lessons.title: Data belongs in the model
paragraphs: A QListView presents data supplied by a model. QAbstractListModel lets you define the rows and roles while keeping the underlying task collection independent of the widget. DisplayRole supplies the title, EditRole supports editing, CheckStateRole presents completion, and UserRole carries a stable UUID.

The sample model reports zero child rows because it is a flat list. It rejects invalid indexes and unsupported roles. Views and tests can ask for data without reaching into the private vector. Changing presentation or adding a second view does not require duplicating task state.
lessons.example:
rowCount(validParent) -> 0
data(index, Qt::DisplayRole) -> title
data(index, Qt::CheckStateRole) -> Checked / Unchecked
data(index, Qt::UserRole) -> stable UUID
lessons.pitfall: Storing the authoritative tasks only as text inside list widgets couples behavior to presentation and makes stable identity harder.

question.prompt: Which value should remain stable when a task changes row position?
question.explanation: Identity belongs to the task rather than its current position.

lessons.title: Bracket structural changes
paragraphs: Views need notifications when row structure changes. Call beginInsertRows before modifying the collection and endInsertRows after it. Removal follows the same contract. For existing values, setData validates the change and emits dataChanged with the affected index and roles.

The model also emits a domain-level changed signal used later for document dirty state. A no-op edit should not produce a new domain change. QAbstractItemModelTester exercises model invariants; QSignalSpy checks intended signals. These complement, rather than replace, assertions about actual stored values.
lessons.pitfall: Mutating the vector before beginInsertRows lets views observe an inconsistent transition and can corrupt selection bookkeeping.

question.prompt: When must beginInsertRows be called?

options.text: Before inserting into the backing collection

question.explanation: The begin/end pair brackets the structural mutation.

lessons.title: Filtering changes the index space
paragraphs: QSortFilterProxyModel can filter and sort a source model without rewriting its data. A visible row belongs to the proxy index space. If the user selects the first visible row after filtering, that row may refer to the third source row. Map the selection before mutating the source.

The task editor sets case-insensitive fixed-string filtering and sorts titles. To delete, it maps list->currentIndex through mapToSource and checks validity. Empty selection must not accidentally become row zero. The tests deliberately filter to a non-first source task and ensure deletion removes that task only.
lessons.example:
QModelIndex source = proxy->mapToSource(list->currentIndex());
if (source.isValid()) model->removeAt(source.row());
lessons.pitfall: Using the proxy row number directly against the source deletes the wrong task after sorting or filtering.

question.prompt: What must happen before deleting a filtered selection from the source model?

options.text: Assume visible row zero is source row zero
Map the proxy index to a source index

question.explanation: Proxy and source positions can differ.

lessons.title: Edits and completion are model operations
paragraphs: Item flags announce whether a row is editable or checkable. setData still enforces the accepted title rule and checks the role. Returning false rejects invalid input without replacing the existing title. Completion changes update the task, notify the view and mark the document changed.

TaskEditor demonstrates inline title edits and checkboxes. Try editing a title so it moves in sorted order, then filter it and toggle completion. Retain identity through those operations. A later undo design would store task identity and old/new values; recording only a transient visible row is unreliable.
lessons.example:
Qt::ItemIsEditable | Qt::ItemIsUserCheckable
setData(index, "Review models", Qt::EditRole)

courses.title: 7. JSON documents and reliable file replacement
courses.summary: Save real local files, validate an entire imported document before replacing state, and recover from cancellation and I/O errors.

lessons.title: Define a versioned document
paragraphs: The task file is a JSON object with version 1 and a tasks array. Each task has a canonical UUID string, a title and a boolean done value. IDs must be unique, titles must pass the same model rules and the array can contain at most 100 tasks. Files are limited to 64 KiB.

JSON parsing proves syntax, not the application schema. A string containing "false" is not the boolean false; a valid number can still be the wrong version. Decode into a temporary vector and reject the whole import when any item fails. This prevents a late malformed row from partially replacing accepted work.
lessons.pitfall: Accepting any parseable JSON allows wrong versions, duplicate identifiers and incompatible field types into the model.

question.prompt: Does successful JSON parsing establish a valid task document?

options.text: Only if the filename ends in .json
No, schema and value validation are still required
Yes, every JSON object is a task document

question.explanation: Syntax and application contracts are different checks.

lessons.title: Bound reads and commit once
paragraphs: Use QFile in read-only mode and read at most the limit plus one byte, which detects oversized files without allocating the entire file. Check read errors and decode the result. The application can ask the user to discard a dirty document before opening another one, but declining or failing to load must retain the current tasks.

TaskFile.h assigns the result vector only after every row is validated. The notebook then replaces the model once. The tests include broken JSON, wrong field types, duplicate IDs and an oversized file, each starting with a known accepted task so state preservation is verified directly.
lessons.pitfall: Appending imported rows while still validating the file creates partial imports when a later row is malformed.

question.prompt: Why decode into a temporary collection?

options.text: To preserve accepted state if any row fails

question.explanation: Validation must finish before committing replacement.

lessons.title: Write, commit and report the outcome
paragraphs: QSaveFile writes through a temporary file and commits a successful replacement. Keep its direct-write fallback disabled so failure to create a temporary file does not silently switch to overwriting the target in place. Check the byte count and commit result before reporting success or clearing dirty state.

This is a local document save strategy, not a database or cloud sync protocol. Filesystem permissions and failures still matter. Test writing to a missing directory, saving valid data and reading the exact bytes back. A success message must describe the actual completed write, while failures leave the in-memory document available.
lessons.pitfall: Treating open success as save success misses short writes and failed commits.

question.prompt: When should the document become clean after Save?

options.text: As soon as the file picker appears
After all bytes are written and commit succeeds

question.explanation: A save is complete only after successful replacement.

lessons.title: User files and preferences are different
paragraphs: The user chooses task documents through file dialogs. QSettings stores small application preferences, such as window geometry, under an application identity. It is not the task-document database. The notebook remembers geometry but does not silently load a task file at startup; Open remains an explicit action.

Use platform path helpers instead of hardcoded C:\ or /Users directories. Later deployment may make the installation directory read-only. Test with a disposable document and profile when trying corruption or permission errors. A path displayed in a status message is useful feedback, but it does not prove the file is readable until a readback succeeds.
lessons.pitfall: Writing user documents beside the executable often fails after installation into a protected application directory.

question.prompt: What belongs in QSettings in this notebook?

options.text: The entire task collection as the only document file

question.explanation: Preferences and user documents have separate persistence roles.

courses.title: 8. SQLite persistence with Qt SQL
courses.summary: Use a real QSQLITE connection, bound queries, transactions and a versioned schema for a small task repository.

lessons.title: A connection is a managed resource
paragraphs: Qt SQL exposes a common API over database drivers. This lab uses QSQLITE and a local SQLite file, not a server. QSqlDatabase is a handle to a named connection. Give each repository instance a distinct name and check open before sending queries; a missing driver is a deployment error worth reporting.

Queries retain connection resources, so destroy them before removing the named connection. The repository scopes queries within operations and closes/releases its own handle before removeDatabase. Use a temporary database in automated tests so previous learner data cannot affect the expected results.
lessons.pitfall: Removing a named connection while queries or copied handles still use it can invalidate ongoing operations.

question.prompt: Which driver does this local database lab use?
question.explanation: QSQLITE connects Qt SQL to a local SQLite database.

lessons.title: Schema versions and stable rows
paragraphs: A tasks table stores an integer primary key, a text title and a checked integer for completion. The title validation rule stays in C++ because database syntax alone does not express every application invariant. PRAGMA user_version records schema version 1; a newer unknown version is rejected rather than guessed at.

The sample creates a new table inside a transaction and sets the version only on success. It does not implement arbitrary upgrades of old databases. A future migration must preserve old data, run transactionally and have fixture tests for every supported starting version. Replacing a table without migration is data loss.
lessons.pitfall: Assuming CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS upgrades an existing schema leaves old columns and constraints unchanged.

question.prompt: What does CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS fail to provide by itself?

options.text: A migration of an existing incompatible table
Creation of any table at all

question.explanation: Existing schema changes require an explicit migration.

lessons.title: Bind values instead of composing SQL
paragraphs: Prepare a statement containing placeholders and bind user values separately. A title containing an apostrophe or SQL-looking text is ordinary data. Never assemble that title into the SQL command. Bound parameters represent values; table and column identifiers still come from fixed application code.

Every prepare, exec and query result should be checked. SELECT returns rows by calling next; an empty result is not the same as a query failure. The repository test inserts a title containing a quote and SQL-looking punctuation, reads it back exactly and checks that the table still contains the expected rows.
lessons.pitfall: Escaping a few apostrophes manually is not a substitute for parameter binding and can miss future input cases.

question.prompt: How should a task title enter an INSERT query?
question.explanation: Binding keeps the value separate from SQL structure.

lessons.title: Commit related work or roll it back
paragraphs: A transaction groups changes into one database decision. Begin it, perform all required operations, then commit. Any failed step should roll back and report failure. The UI refreshes from successfully stored rows rather than assuming an attempted insert succeeded. This avoids phantom tasks when disk or database operations fail.

SQLite is suitable for this small local repository, but synchronous database work can still block the GUI if it grows large. A background repository must create and use its connection in the appropriate thread and return data to the UI. The lesson stays bounded and demonstrates persistence across process restarts.

transaction -> validated insert -> successful exec -> commit
any failure -> rollback -> keep current view
refresh -> SELECT rows -> update displayed list
lessons.pitfall: Updating the UI as if a transaction committed can show tasks that do not exist in the database after a failure.

question.prompt: What should a failed multi-step transaction do?

options.text: Commit its first successful statement silently
Roll back and expose the failure

question.explanation: Atomic operations preserve the previous committed state on failure.

courses.title: 9. Asynchronous HTTP and bounded replies
courses.summary: Build a real Qt Network client against a loopback fixture, with response validation, cancellation and clear error states.

lessons.title: Requests are asynchronous operations
paragraphs: QNetworkAccessManager starts requests without blocking the GUI until a response arrives. A QNetworkReply reports headers, incoming data, errors and completion. The manager and its replies belong to their QObject thread; normal asynchronous network I/O does not require a custom worker thread.

This lesson calls a fixed loopback URL only when Fetch is clicked. Run the included Python fixture locally to supply JSON; it does not contact an external service or require credentials. A future production client needs its own endpoint contract and HTTPS configuration. Never disable TLS certificate validation to hide a connection failure.
lessons.pitfall: Calling a blocking wait loop in the GUI defeats the asynchronous request design and makes Cancel inaccessible.

question.prompt: Does ordinary QNetworkAccessManager I/O need a custom worker thread?

options.text: Only if the response is JSON
No, it already provides asynchronous request handling
Yes, every GET needs its own QThread

question.explanation: The manager integrates network progress with its event loop.

lessons.title: Limit time, bytes and concurrency
paragraphs: A responsive client needs explicit resource policies. This project allows one active request, a two-second absolute deadline and at most 4096 response bytes. Read incrementally, stop when the cap is exceeded, and abort on deadline or Cancel. Content-Length alone is not a reliable allocation limit.

Redirects are rejected in this fixed local fixture client so a response cannot silently change the destination contract. The sample does not automatically retry a failed request. Its status distinguishes busy, cancelled, oversized, timed out and completed operations. The UI re-enables Fetch only when the active reply completes.
lessons.example:
readyRead -> read up to remaining bytes + 1
size > 4096 -> abort and report oversize
deadline -> abort
Cancel -> abort
finished -> settle once
lessons.pitfall: Reading an arbitrary response with readAll before checking its size defeats the intended memory bound.

question.prompt: Why count received bytes even when Content-Length is present?

options.text: The actual received body must obey the limit
Content-Length always includes the JSON schema

question.explanation: Headers do not replace enforcement while reading.

lessons.title: Transport success is not valid data
paragraphs: Check network error state and the HTTP status before accepting a response. A successful request can return malformed JSON or the wrong schema. This client expects an object containing a string message of bounded length and displays that message as plain text. Errors never replace it with invented success data.

The loopback fixture emits a fixed response so you can predict the first result. Native tests substitute local responses for HTTP errors, malformed JSON and excessive bodies. This verifies both the transport path and the validation decision without relying on an unstable public API.
lessons.example:
HTTP 200 + {"message":"Hello from the local Qt fixture"} -> accept
HTTP 404 -> error
HTTP 200 + {"message":17} -> schema error
lessons.pitfall: Treating finished as success skips HTTP and schema validation; finished also occurs after errors and aborts.

question.prompt: What does a reply finished signal guarantee?

options.text: That the response is a task document
The operation ended, not that its data is valid

question.explanation: Completion and successful validation are separate conditions.

lessons.title: Settle and release the reply
paragraphs: A reply is a QObject resource. Connect callbacks with a live context, settle the operation once, then schedule deleteLater rather than deleting it inside its own signal handler. A deadline timer parented to the reply disappears with it. Destroying the client also disposes its manager and outstanding reply.

The sample prevents overlapping requests rather than implementing newest-response arbitration. If you extend it to live search, assign a generation to each request so an older completion cannot overwrite newer results. Cancel is an actual abort request here; do not label merely hiding a result as network cancellation.
lessons.pitfall: Deleting a reply immediately inside its finished handler can conflict with the signal delivery lifecycle.

question.prompt: Which cleanup belongs in the reply completion handler?

options.text: Schedule deleteLater after processing the result

question.explanation: Deferred deletion releases the object at an appropriate event-loop point.

courses.title: 10. Background work and cooperative cancellation
courses.summary: Run bounded CPU work with QtConcurrent, keep Widgets on the GUI thread, and make cancellation and shutdown explicit.

lessons.title: Work and widgets have different threads
paragraphs: A GUI callback runs in the GUI thread unless a deliberate delivery boundary changes that. Long CPU work belongs outside that event loop. QtConcurrent::run can execute a callable on a thread pool, but the callable must not manipulate Widgets. Return a value and let the GUI consume it after completion.

The sample sums integers from 1 to N using an owned integer limit and a shared cancellation flag. No input widget pointer crosses into the worker. A QFutureWatcher observes completion in the GUI context. This is a responsiveness experiment; the displayed sum is real arithmetic, but no native speedup claim is made.
lessons.pitfall: Capturing a QWidget pointer and calling setText from the worker violates the GUI thread boundary.

question.prompt: Where should the worker update a QLabel?

options.text: It should return data and let the GUI update the label

question.explanation: Widgets must be accessed in their GUI thread.

lessons.title: Cancellation needs cooperation
paragraphs: In basic QtConcurrent::run, asking a future to cancel does not automatically stop an arbitrary callable. This project passes a shared atomic boolean and checks it at bounded intervals inside the loop. Cancel sets that flag. The worker returns a cancellation result at its next checkpoint.

The limit is at most 100 million and the sum uses an unsigned 64-bit accumulator. Cancellation is best effort at checkpoints, not an immediate kill. Do not hold locks while updating the UI, and do not use forced thread termination to avoid designing a clean exit path.
lessons.pitfall: A Cancel button that only changes its label leaves the expensive operation running and misrepresents its behavior.

question.prompt: What makes this worker stop after Cancel?

options.text: Its periodic check of the shared atomic flag

question.explanation: The callable explicitly cooperates with the cancellation request.

lessons.title: Owned state survives the callback
paragraphs: The worker owns copies of its input and a shared pointer to the cancellation flag. The window owns the watcher, and all UI callbacks use the window as context. Destroying the window requests cancellation and disconnects UI callbacks; the worker never dereferences the destroyed window.

Only one job is allowed at a time. Start is disabled until the existing job settles, so an old job cannot overwrite a newer job in this implementation. A design that permits overlapping jobs must additionally track request identity. Thread-pool shutdown may wait for active work, which is why bounded work and cancellation checkpoints matter.
lessons.pitfall: Capturing local references or this in the background callable can create a use-after-destruction when the user closes the window.

question.prompt: What should the background callable own?

options.text: A reference to a temporary local input
A raw pointer to a destroyed window
Copies of its data and a shared cancellation state

question.explanation: Owned data separates worker lifetime from UI lifetime.

lessons.title: Prove arithmetic and responsiveness separately
paragraphs: For N=1000 the sum is 500500. A reference formula checks the worker result independently of the loop. Test cancellation with a flag set before work begins, and test the GUI completion path with an actual future. Use signal-driven waiting rather than fixed sleeps that guess how fast the host is.

Manual checks include resizing during work, pressing Cancel and closing while work is active. Those observations establish interaction behavior on the tested host. They do not establish that another machine has the same timing. A benchmark would need a different experimental design with workload sizes, repeated samples and documented hardware.
lessons.example:
reference = N * (N + 1) / 2
N = 1000 -> 500500
cancellation requested before run -> cancelled result
GUI remains available while the future is pending
lessons.pitfall: A test that only checks the Start button text proves neither arithmetic correctness nor completion delivery.

question.prompt: Which is independent evidence of arithmetic correctness?

options.text: Check that the Cancel button is green
Compare the worker sum to N*(N+1)/2

question.explanation: An independent expected value can catch an incorrect loop.

courses.title: 11. Custom painting and scalable visual feedback
courses.summary: Build a QPainter progress view with an accessible numerical control, resize-aware geometry and honest rendering tests.

lessons.title: Painting is a response to state
paragraphs: A custom QWidget receives paintEvent when its pixels need to be drawn. Store the value separately, and let paintEvent read it to draw the current view. QPainter belongs inside the painting operation for a widget; do not keep a widget painter alive between events.

The lesson draws a progress bar and a numerical percentage. A standard slider controls the value. Changing the value calls update, which schedules a repaint through Qt rather than drawing directly inside the input handler. Multiple update requests can be combined by the event loop.
lessons.pitfall: Painting in a button handler instead of paintEvent can disappear when the window is covered, exposed or resized.

question.prompt: How should an input change request a widget redraw?

options.text: Keep a permanent QPainter on the widget
Write pixels only in the slider callback

question.explanation: Qt repaints from state when a paint event is delivered.

lessons.title: Derive drawing from the available rectangle
paragraphs: Use the widget rectangle to compute margins, track width and fill width. A 25 percent value fills one quarter of the usable track, not one quarter of a fixed design screenshot. Clamp the input and guard small rectangles so geometry never becomes negative.

Qt generally exposes logical drawing coordinates while the platform handles device scaling. Avoid multiplying every widget coordinate by a guessed DPI factor. Test several sizes and scale settings on actual targets. Vector shapes and text should stay aligned when the widget resizes.
lessons.pitfall: Hardcoding a 600-pixel track makes a smaller window clip the meaningful part of the drawing.

question.prompt: What should determine progress-bar width?

options.text: Only the size of the author's monitor
The current widget rectangle and value

question.explanation: Drawing should respond to available space.

lessons.title: A drawing needs a usable equivalent
paragraphs: A painted shape does not automatically expose all its meaning to keyboard users or assistive technology. Keep an ordinary slider and a text percentage with accessible names. The slider provides keyboard input while the label communicates the numeric value independently of color.

The custom widget is a view of that value, not the sole interface. Use sufficient contrast and a stable label. For a complex interactive custom control, implement the appropriate accessibility interface and verify with native assistive tools; this introductory widget deliberately leaves input to a standard control.

QSlider -> keyboard-editable value 0..100
QLabel -> literal "Progress: 25%"
QPainter -> visual track and fill
lessons.pitfall: Encoding completion only by color excludes users who cannot perceive that color or inspect the painting.

question.explanation: A standard input complements the custom drawing.

lessons.title: Verify state and rendering boundaries
paragraphs: Test that input clamps to 0..100, that the text label matches the value and that rendering at different sizes produces a nonempty image. Those are useful checks but they do not certify every pixel, font or screen-reader experience. Manual inspection still checks clipping and focus visibility.

Use deterministic values such as 0, 25 and 100. Inspect the resulting image and compare the numerical meaning. A blank screenshot is a rendering failure, while a correct label paired with a reversed fill is a visualization failure. Both state and visual output deserve an explicit check.

assert numeric text is Progress: 25%
inspect track: fill occupies one quarter of usable width

question.explanation: The visual must represent the actual underlying value.

courses.title: 12. Qt Quick, QML and a C++ backend
courses.summary: Build a real QML desktop window with declarative bindings, Qt Quick Controls and typed C++ property notifications.

lessons.title: Widgets and Qt Quick are different UI systems
paragraphs: Qt Widgets suits conventional desktop forms and mature widget-based applications. Qt Quick uses QML to describe a scene of items and bindings, with Qt Quick Controls providing higher-level controls. Both can use C++ application logic; learning QML does not mean rewriting the model in browser JavaScript.

This project uses QGuiApplication and QQmlApplicationEngine, a Main.qml resource and a C++ CounterBackend. It is a native Qt Quick app. CMake registers the QML module under VoltQuest.Lesson. The browser course viewer only displays these files; it does not execute the QML or replace native rendering.

C++ backend -> properties and invokable methods
QML -> layout, controls, bindings
QQmlApplicationEngine -> loads VoltQuest.Lesson/Main

lessons.title: Expose a small C++ API
paragraphs: A Q_PROPERTY declares the value QML can read and identifies its NOTIFY signal. The backend exposes count and an invokable increment method. Changing the stored value emits countChanged so QML can re-evaluate expressions depending on it. Keep internal ownership and mutable collections behind a deliberate API.

The source uses QML_ELEMENT with qt_add_qml_module to register CounterBackend as a module type. The QML file creates a backend instance and calls its method when a button is activated. A property that changes without notification leaves dependent bindings stale even though the C++ value is correct.

lessons.title: Bindings describe relationships
paragraphs: A binding such as text: "Count: " + counter.count expresses how text depends on a property. It updates when the dependency notifies. An imperative assignment to the text property can replace that binding; if the label stops following count after a manual assignment, inspect whether the relationship was removed.

Use layouts and explicit preferred dimensions to make controls adapt. The sample button invokes increment and lets the label binding do the rendering. QML IDs name objects within their component scope; objectName is a separate runtime property used by the native test to find an object deliberately.
lessons.pitfall: Setting countLabel.text manually after each click duplicates a relationship that should remain a binding.

options.text: Automatically create a new C++ thread

question.explanation: A direct assignment can remove the original dependency expression.

lessons.title: Package and test the module
paragraphs: qt_add_qml_module records the module URI, QML files and C++ types, and places the resources where the engine can resolve them. loadFromModule uses the module URI and root type name. Check engine root objects after loading and fail startup if the window could not be created.

The native test loads the actual module, invokes the C++ increment method and checks the QML label changes. Deployment must include Qt Quick, Controls, platform plugins and QML imports in addition to the executable. A successful Widgets deployment is not proof that a QML app has all its runtime modules.
lessons.example:
qt_add_qml_module(app
    URI VoltQuest.Lesson
    QML_FILES Main.qml
    SOURCES CounterBackend.h)
engine.loadFromModule("VoltQuest.Lesson", "Main");
lessons.pitfall: Shipping only the executable misses QML imports and runtime dependencies needed on a clean machine.

question.prompt: What extra deployment concern does the QML app introduce?

options.text: Its QML imports and Qt Quick runtime modules

question.explanation: The native runtime must locate the module dependencies.

courses.title: 13. Translation, keyboard access and preferences
courses.summary: Ship English/Indonesian native UI text, preserve drafts when language changes, and verify keyboard and accessibility behavior.

lessons.title: Separate interface strings from user data
paragraphs: Wrap interface messages in a consistent translation context so lupdate can collect them into a .ts catalogue. Translate the messages, then compile that catalogue into a .qm resource using lrelease. User titles, identifiers and saved task data should not be translated just because the interface language changes.

The native sample includes lesson_id.ts and builds the actual Indonesian translation resource. Its text field contains a learner draft. The language button switches interface labels while preserving that draft exactly. The browser course controls have their own Indonesian translations; they are separate from these downloadable native Qt resources.

source text -> lupdate -> lesson_id.ts
translated catalogue -> lrelease -> lesson_id.qm
QTranslator loads the compiled resource

question.prompt: Which text should the native translator leave unchanged?
question.explanation: Application interface messages and user-authored content have different roles.

lessons.title: Install a translator with a live lifetime
paragraphs: QTranslator must remain alive while installed. Load the compiled resource, check success and install it on the application. Removing it restores source-language lookup. Existing widgets need their visible strings refreshed when the language changes; changing the translator does not rewrite every previously assigned QString automatically.

The sample keeps a translator as a window member, handles LanguageChange and calls its translation function for labels and accessible names. It removes the translator during teardown. A failed resource load reports an error instead of claiming the language was switched. The input widget is never reconstructed.
lessons.pitfall: A translator created as a short-lived local variable disappears immediately after the switching function returns.

question.prompt: What lifetime must an installed QTranslator have?

options.text: It may be destroyed immediately after installTranslator
It exists only during CMake configure
It must remain alive while in use

question.explanation: Translation lookup relies on the live translator object.

lessons.title: Keyboard and accessible names are behavior
paragraphs: Provide persistent labels, buddies and meaningful accessible names. Use standard controls for editing and activation so platform keyboard behavior is available. A translated label can require more room, and a keyboard mnemonic may need a different letter in the translated message.

Test the entire task with Tab and activation keys, at a larger font and with native assistive technology. Automated tests can inspect labels, buddy relationships and preserved values, but those tests do not establish a complete screen-reader experience. Record which OS, scale and assistive tool were actually exercised.
lessons.example:
English: &Task title -> buddy input
Indonesian: &Judul tugas -> same input
Existing draft and selection remain in that input.
lessons.pitfall: Recreating controls during language changes can erase input, selection, focus and signal connections.

question.prompt: Why update labels in place during a language switch?

options.text: To preserve the existing input and interaction state

question.explanation: The same controls can retain their values and focus.

lessons.title: Preferences need an explicit scope
paragraphs: Store a chosen language or geometry under the application's QSettings identity if persistence is part of the feature. Define what happens when a saved choice is unavailable. The native translation sample switches during the current run; persisting the language is the applied extension. The notebook sample already stores geometry separately from documents.

A preference failure should not make the main task unusable. Avoid using a global application name shared with unrelated programs, and use a disposable test profile when exercising preferences. Restart tests are necessary before claiming that a choice persists across launches; an in-memory toggle alone does not prove persistence.
lessons.example:
organization + application identity -> QSettings scope
language choice -> optional preference
task titles -> user document, unchanged
lessons.pitfall: Claiming language persistence from a same-window toggle test confuses in-memory state with a completed disk round trip.

question.prompt: What is needed to prove a language preference survives restart?

options.text: Store it, restart and observe the restored choice

question.explanation: Persistence requires a new application lifetime and readback.

Enter an unfinished title, switch to Indonesian and confirm the title remains exact.

courses.title: 14. Qt Test, debugging and regression design
courses.summary: Test real user actions, model invariants and document failures with deterministic fixtures and inspectable diagnostics.

lessons.title: Choose the boundary the test must prove
paragraphs: A validator test checks accepted data rules. A model test checks row transitions, notifications and identity. A UI test activates controls and observes application state. A file test writes and reads a temporary document. Each catches a different class of defect; testing only one layer leaves integration mistakes invisible.

The course project is the task notebook plus a more extensive Qt Test suite. It uses the exact same headers as the runnable application. Test fixtures use QTemporaryDir and known task values. Start every case from explicit data so a prior run cannot make a failure disappear.
lessons.example:
rules -> blank/control/length boundaries
model -> insert/edit/remove and proxy identity
UI -> actual button/key actions
file -> exact round trip and failed replacement
lessons.pitfall: Writing a test that duplicates the implementation's loop can reproduce the same mistake instead of independently checking behavior.

question.prompt: Why exercise the UI in addition to the model?

options.text: To make all tests depend on screenshots
To verify controls actually invoke the intended model behavior

question.explanation: A correct model can still be wired to the wrong action.

lessons.title: Observe signals and wait for conditions
paragraphs: QSignalSpy records real signal emissions and their arguments. It can prove that one action causes one notification or that a rejected edit emits none. For asynchronous work, wait for an observable condition using QTRY_VERIFY or an appropriate signal wait rather than sleeping a guessed number of milliseconds.

QAbstractItemModelTester checks model consistency while your assertions check domain expectations. A green test report should identify what ran. An offscreen widget test can validate interactions and painting without proving the operating system's native dialogs, GPU behavior or assistive-tool experience.
lessons.pitfall: A fixed sleep can be too short on a slower host and unnecessarily long on a faster one.

question.prompt: What should an asynchronous test wait for?

options.text: A different source file to appear
An arbitrary delay chosen from one laptop

question.explanation: Condition-based waiting follows the behavior being tested.

lessons.title: Debug the first divergent state
paragraphs: Use a Debug build, set a breakpoint before mutation and inspect the input, model state and expected transition. If an operation changes the wrong task after filtering, inspect both proxy and source indexes. If a save reports success incorrectly, follow the open/write/commit outcomes.

Read the first relevant compiler or runtime diagnostic and keep a small reproduction. Log useful operation outcomes without dumping private user documents. A failing assertion is evidence: preserve it while fixing the code, then run the same case again to demonstrate the regression is addressed.
lessons.example:
reproduce -> inspect input -> expected state -> actual state
filtered remove: proxy row 0 may map to source row 2
save failure: dirty must remain true
lessons.pitfall: Changing many unrelated lines before locating the first divergence can hide the defect and make the regression hard to explain.

question.prompt: What is the most useful first debugging target?

options.text: The first state that differs from the expected transition

question.explanation: Find where the behavior first departs from the contract.

lessons.title: Make verification claims match evidence
paragraphs: CTest can run the native suite after CMake builds it. Keep test failures visible in command output and ensure Release builds do not remove all checks through disabled assert macros. Qt Test uses its own assertion macros. A release checklist records actual platform, Qt kit and package results.

The supplied tests exercise the notebook on the current host. Cross-platform source does not prove binaries for every platform. Native file dialogs, installer behavior, scaling, keyboard conventions and accessibility require target checks. The course certificate records self-study exam completion, not independent native application certification.
lessons.example:
cmake --build build --config Debug
ctest --test-dir build -C Debug --output-on-failure
# Repeat relevant tests on each supported target and package.
lessons.pitfall: Reporting a successful source scan as a successful native launch overstates what was actually verified.

question.prompt: What does a browser course exam pass establish?

options.text: That the learner's binary is signed and installed on every OS
That every native test was executed

question.explanation: Assessment and native application verification are separate records.

courses.title: 15. Release builds and desktop deployment
courses.summary: Create a native install tree, include runtime resources, and plan target-specific packaging, signing and update verification.

lessons.title: An executable is only part of the application
paragraphs: A development machine can find Qt libraries through its installed kit, which hides missing package dependencies. A release artifact needs the executable plus the required libraries, platform plugins and resources. QML applications also need their imported modules. The deployment example embeds a text resource and displays its content.

Build a Release configuration and install into a staging directory. Launch from that directory with an unrelated working directory. A resource referenced through the Qt resource system should still resolve; a relative file accidentally found in the source folder should not be required for startup.
lessons.example:
source folder != build folder != install staging folder
resource URL: :/lesson/about.txt
launch staged executable from a different working directory
lessons.pitfall: A launch that succeeds only while the current directory is the source tree can conceal a missing packaged resource.

question.prompt: Why launch the staged app from an unrelated directory?

options.text: To detect accidental dependence on source-tree relative paths

question.explanation: The package should contain or locate its own runtime resources.

lessons.title: Use the tools for the target kit
paragraphs: The CMake install rules define where the executable goes. Qt deployment helpers inspect runtime dependencies and generate an install script on supported host/target combinations. The lesson exposes this through the VQ_DEPLOY option. A configuration that does not support the helper must fail visibly rather than pretending deployment succeeded.

Windows uses a matching compiler runtime and Qt plugins, commonly assembled with windeployqt or the CMake deployment helper. macOS bundles need the appropriate frameworks/plugins and later signing. Linux packaging must account for the target distribution and system-library compatibility. One host cannot establish all three outcomes.
lessons.example:
cmake -S . -B release -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DVQ_DEPLOY=ON
cmake --build release --config Release
cmake --install release --config Release --prefix stage
lessons.pitfall: Copying arbitrary DLLs from a different kit can mix architectures or Qt versions and create difficult runtime failures.

question.prompt: Which Qt libraries should deployment use?

options.text: Those matching the built target's Qt kit
Whatever DLLs are newest on the internet

question.explanation: Runtime libraries, plugins and the application must be compatible.

lessons.title: Signing, licenses and updates are release work
paragraphs: A staged directory is not yet a signed installer or an update service. Platform signing, notarization or package metadata depends on the distribution method. Record exactly what has been produced: source ZIP, compiled binary, installed bundle or signed release package. Check the terms for the Qt modules and other dependencies you redistribute.

An update must preserve user files and settings, so keep user data outside the installation tree. Test an upgrade using a copy of real versioned data, and define how the older app responds to a newer document schema. This course provides a checklist and build rules, not automatic signing credentials or a production updater.
lessons.example:
release record:
Qt kit + compiler + architecture + build type
package contents + dependency notices
fresh install + upgrade with existing user data

options.text: Editable source requiring a native build

question.explanation: Artifact names should describe what was actually produced.

lessons.title: Validate a clean target and failure recovery
paragraphs: Run the package on a clean machine or VM without the development kit supplying missing files. Verify launch, resources, keyboard input, dialogs, file read/write and normal shutdown. For QML also check module loading; for SQLite check the driver plugin. Record logs and actual versions in RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md.

Clean-target testing is distinct from running CTest on the build host. Make a backup of sample user data before an upgrade rehearsal and verify it afterward. A failed deployment must be reported as a failure, not worked around by silently depending on an unrelated Qt installation.

fresh target -> launch -> resources -> interactions -> save/readback
upgrade target -> existing data retained -> old/new schema policy
record PASS / FAIL / NOT RUN for each target

courses.title: 16. Capstone: a Qt desktop task manager
courses.summary: Integrate validated task editing, filtering, completion, JSON documents, unsaved-work protection, preferences and a native regression suite.

lessons.title: Assemble the boundaries into one application
paragraphs: The capstone combines Task.h for accepted data, TaskModel for rows and notifications, TaskEditor for controls, TaskFile for versioned JSON, and Notebook for document actions. The GUI remains a view/controller layer around those contracts. A task has a stable UUID even when its title or visible position changes.

The shipped capstone supports add, inline rename, completion checkboxes, sorted text filtering, removal, New, Open, Save and Save As. It uses JSON documents and geometry preferences. The SQLite, HTTP, background-work and QML courses are separate working examples; integrating those features into this notebook is optional extension work, not a claim about the shipped capstone.
lessons.example:
Task -> TaskModel -> filter proxy -> QListView
TaskEditor -> validated model operations
Notebook -> dirty state and document commands
TaskFile -> bounded parse / validated replacement / committed save
lessons.pitfall: Trying to combine every technology before defining ownership and data contracts makes failures hard to isolate.

question.prompt: Which storage mechanism does the shipped capstone use for documents?
question.explanation: The capstone deliberately has an inspectable local document contract.

lessons.title: Preserve identity through user workflows
paragraphs: Add Zebra, Alpha and Middle; sorting changes the visible order while IDs remain attached to the accepted tasks. Filter to Middle, edit it, toggle completion and remove it. Selection must map through the proxy. Filtering hides rows without deleting or rewriting them in the source model.

The title input is a draft until Add succeeds. Save writes accepted tasks only and says that an unadded draft is not included. New, Open and Close guard both dirty accepted tasks and nonempty input drafts before discarding work. This distinction prevents a clean model from concealing an unsaved draft.
lessons.example:
accepted tasks != current unadded input
Save -> accepted tasks only
New/Open/Close -> protect dirty tasks and nonempty input
filter -> presentation only
lessons.pitfall: Checking only model dirty state can discard an unadded input draft even though the task collection has not changed.

question.prompt: What must Close protect besides dirty accepted tasks?
question.explanation: The user may have unsaved work before it becomes an accepted task.

lessons.title: Round-trip and recover from failures
paragraphs: Save a document, keep its bytes as evidence, mutate the in-memory state and reload the saved version. IDs, titles and done values must survive the round trip. Now try invalid JSON, a duplicate UUID, more than 100 tasks and a file above 64 KiB; none should replace the accepted document.

A failed save keeps accepted task changes dirty. A successful Save As changes the current path only after commit. Cancelling a file dialog leaves the previous path and data alone. Window geometry uses QSettings and does not substitute for an explicit task-document save. These are behavior contracts, not just menu labels.
lessons.example:
valid save -> commit -> current path changes -> model clean
failed save -> path unchanged -> dirty unchanged
invalid open -> existing tasks unchanged
valid open -> one validated replacement
lessons.pitfall: Setting the current filename before Save As succeeds can make subsequent Save overwrite the wrong destination after a failure.

question.prompt: When should Save As adopt its new current path?
question.explanation: The active document path should follow a completed save.

lessons.title: Deliver a reviewable desktop application
paragraphs: Use the included Qt Test suite to establish critical state transitions and failure handling. Run the app manually to review keyboard flow, focus after adding a task, inline editing and document dialogs. Fill in the release checklist with actual host and target results, including what remains untested.

For an extension choose one coherent addition: undo commands keyed by stable ID, a versioned priority field, a SQLite-backed repository, or a QML view of the same domain model. Define the added contract and tests before claiming it is part of the shipped notebook. Finish with a reproducible source pack, build instructions and retained data examples.

release artifact + honest target checklist
